lines: On one Microsoft Store launch, I surfaced four hundred craft and implementation issues in review, from line heights and spacing to loaders and dark-mode colors.
They were found by eye, after the feature was built.
Every issue meant the same round trip: spot the mismatch, screenshot it, write it up, file a bug, then check the fix.
The feedback was scattered across Figma, Loop and the bug tracker, and the designer stayed the last quality gate.
Some craft decisions need a designer.
So I moved the check before the designer's review. Engineers drop in the design and the build, and run it.
There's no setup. Two screenshots are enough to start.
Each check runs two engines. First, a pixel-level color diff catches exact hex mismatches.
Then an AI vision model compares both screens for copy, spacing and missing elements, the things a pixel diff can't explain.
Every issue names the property, the design value, and the built value.
Hover an issue, and its region lights up on the build. Filters let designers and engineers each focus on what matters to them.
Then it goes straight into the team's workflow.
One click files a pre-filled bug in Azure DevOps, or copies every issue into Loop as a ready table.
I built Craft Check on my own with AI: a React app with Fluent UI, a server, and a command line tool that also compares Figma tokens with CSS and Windows XAML.
It's a working prototype, which I took to Microsoft's F H L hackathon in March twenty twenty-six. Next, direct Figma integration, then running the check automatically before code is merged.
Automate the measuring, so designers can spend their time on judgment.
